course_details.Overview of class: Medieval men and women journeyed astonishing distances by foot, pack animals, and boat for trade, religion, diplomacy, and the love of exploration. In the tenth century, a Muslim traveler from Baghdad journeyed up the Volga and brought news of the Vikings back home. Centuries later, the Venetian Marco Polo wrote about, and also likely lied about, traveling Asia and his time at the court of Kublai Khan. Ethiopian merchants traveled to the courts of Italy searching for Christian relics to bring back to Africa, and Eurocentric maps and travelogues imagined distant spaces as peopled with so-called monstrous races, like the cynocephali (dog-headed people). For many medieval peoples, marvelous beasts, terrifying sea monsters, and fantastic mines of gems dotted the edges of their maps, and similar ideas about what was familiar and what was exotic deeply informed premodern notions of race and empire. This class investigates a wealth of travel writings and artifacts like these by enigmatic authors from all Abrahamic faiths—Christianity, Judaism, and Islam—in order to consider what happens when people from distinct cultures meet for the first time. By following in the footsteps of such intrepid explorers, we witness how medieval people crafted narratives that strategically shaped understandings of the unknown, and the way their writings informed broader histories of race-making, religion, empire, and borders.

course_details.Overview of class:
Since the 19th century, archaeology has played a pivotal role in the politics of the modern Middle East. As nation-states emerged, leaders and intellectuals often turned to the ancient past to construct and legitimize national identities. Archaeological discoveries were used to create narratives that linked contemporary populations to illustrious ancient civilizations, thereby fostering a sense of pride and continuity. This instrumentalization of archaeology served political agendas, reinforcing territorial claims and cultural heritage.
In this course, we will explore the complicated relationship between archaeology, politics, and national identity in the modern Middle East, tracing how this relationship has changed over time. Through a series of case studies from various countries and time periods, we will study how archaeological discoveries and interpretations have been instrumentalized to serve political agendas, shape cultural narratives, and construct national identities. Working with primary and secondary sources (such as official documents, images, and artifacts), we will consider the conditions under which historical actors operated, analyze causes and consequences, and compare continuities and ruptures across cases. We will critically examine the role of archaeology in contemporary political discourse and its impact on regional and global perceptions of the Middle East. The course will include a field trip to the ISAC Museum of the University of Chicago, where we will engage directly with the materials, cultures, and places we study.

course_details.Overview of class: Modernity has dramatically changed the profile of Western Civilization and had a major impact on the European Jews. The course will take students from French Revolution that started integrating the Jews into the fabric of European society to the establishment of the State of Israel. It will highlight the plurality of models of Jewish integration and acculturation, the formation of new Jewish identities, the split of the traditional community under the impact of Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment), the rise of Liberal and Orthodox trends within Judaism, and the spread of Jewish political movements such as socialism and nationalism. Based on a plethora of English-language documents, the course will introduce students to those problems of interaction between the general society and the Jewish minority that pointed toward the twentieth century transformation of modernity. In sum, the course will explore the fascinating response of Jews to modernity on political, societal, theological, and cultural levels.

course_details.Overview of class:
The United States emerged through wars, it expanded through wars, and war created its institutions, forged its social order, fueled its economy, and stamped its politics and culture. Americans have defined who they are in large part by waging war, with sweeping consequences for themselves and others.

Yet as with all things so ubiquitous, war often goes unnoticed. Like our shadow, it is always with us yet seldom noticed; like the sun, it can be painful to look at directly. Arguably that is why some wish to bring war back--and bring it "home"--as they attempt to recreate the nation through war.

course_details.Overview of class: This course examines two institutions - the prison and the detention camp - that traditionally have been studied separately. At the course's foundation lies a hypothesis: the practice of imprisoning masses of people for extended periods of time is both a product of the modern state and a constituent element of the modern era. Every modern state has its own prison system to remove those it deems criminal from society. Over the past two centuries numerous regimes have resorted to detention camps in one form or another: to confine allegedly rebellious peoples, feared minorities, enemy soldiers, or stateless refugees. With varying degrees of brutality and murderous intent - a critical consideration the course will always keep in mind - those in power have used prisons and camps to suppress racial, religious, political, and other identified groups, and to exploit their labor for public and private use. Authorities have mandated that the condemned toil in confinement to pay a debt to society and for their own rehabilitation. Regardless of the great variety of pretexts under which regimes have imprisoned citizens and subjects, both modern structures of incarceration and the experience of the incarcerated bear a great number of similarities that this course will explore and discuss. The course begins with a consideration of alternate forms of punishment common to the premodern era and then follows the development and spread of the modern prison and the proliferation of mass detention camps across the globe over the course of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. We will seek to understand the prisoner experience (to the extent possible) and discuss the place of bounded sites of detention in governance, justice, repression, societal relations, and, ultimately, tourism.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The course introduces students to the intertwined histories of the modern prison and various types of detention camps (concentration, reeducation, forced labor, refugee) that became ubiquitous over the course of the modern era. With an eye to both similarity and difference, the course aims to investigate these developments from an integrated global perspective in an effort to understand the ideas behind the implementation of specific systems of confinement and the lived experience of those confined. Students will read a variety of sources, including primary witness accounts, and employ them in class discussions and written assignments to craft original historical arguments.

course_details.Overview of class: You have heard this before: Africa is the most culturally diverse continent, with more than 1,500 languages. It has the longest record of human history. In fact, it is the birthplace of humankind! What's more, the continent is home to some of the profound experiments and innovations in sociopolitical organization over the past 12,000 years. This course introduces students to the deep history of Africa and its people through the lens of governance—the practices, beliefs, dialogues, and institutions for managing and organizing societies and maintaining social order. We will use case studies from different parts of this storied continent to explore how ancestral Africans organized themselves, conceptualized governance, and negotiated power at different scales, from village level to empires. We will investigate how they managed environmental changes, food security, population growth, migration, diversity, wellness, and both abundance and scarcity. In the process, what debates did these ancestral Africans generate about human rights, social responsibilities, moral communities, balance of power, and democratic principles? What roles did gender, knowledge, and technology play in shaping power and governance in these different African case studies? Students will learn how to use a diverse set of primary sources, including material culture, epics, texts, and artworks, to answer these questions. Apart from eliciting and satisfying the curiosity of students about African history, the course is particularly useful for students who plan to pursue a career in development, teaching and education, academics, social policy, law, journalism, politics, global business, healthcare, cultural affairs, heritage and museum studies, community organizing, travel and hospitality, and international studies.

course_details.Registration Requirements:
How have women shaped ideas about religion, ethical conduct, and identity in the modern Muslim world? This seminar explores Muslim women's voices at two critical juncture in modern history—the transition from Muslim empires to European imperialism and then from European rule to post-colonial sovereignty. Although ‘Islam' is often believed to justify oppression of women and regulation of their public lives in theological terms, this seminar is an opportunity to dig deeper into Islamic intellectual movements that continue to shape how Muslim women and Islam are perceived to this day. Our goal is to historicize such common perceptions, rather than accept them as commonsensical or dismiss them as obvious stereotypes. This entails reflection using gender as an analytical category to study the historical intersections among Islam, modernity, and colonialism.
The course is divided into two parts. Part One focuses on ideological responses to historical transformations, most notably the onset of imperialism and then post-colonial nationhood, in various parts of the Muslim world. To contextualize our understanding of these intellectual currents, Part II focuses on South Asia which is home to one of the world's largest Muslim populations today. Based on texts composed by Muslim women and Muslim male theologians, we will consider themes such as religious and intellectual change, women's social and economic rights, and feminism in Islam. Throughout this course, we will elucidate the complexity and historical dynamism of Islamic intellectual traditions, and discover the nuanced ways in which Muslim women have become agents of their own change while navigating multiple forms of authority and power in Muslim societies.

course_details.Overview of class:
With a warming rate double the global average and half of the world's oil reserves, the Middle East is a
pivotal site for understanding the history, present, and future of climate change. Although Israel/Palestine
is not today an oil-producing country, historically it was imagined differently: in the 19th and 20th
centuries it was considered a promising frontier for oil exploration and became a regional hub of fossil fuel
infrastructures, channeling Middle Eastern oil and North African gas to Europe. This seminar examines
how the rise of fossil fuels and the dynamics of climate change played out in Palestine/Israel and shaped
both the Zionist-Palestinian struggle and Palestine's place within the Middle East. We will consider how
the Middle East became "Middle" through the interplay between energy sources, infrastructures, and
colonial powers. We will explore how carbonization in the region gave rise to new forms of political rule,
reshaping identities and altering environments, and how seemingly mundane infrastructures - from
coaling depots to automobility - enabled and managed colonial power as well as resistance to it. Drawing
on archival materials alongside fiction, poetry, and film in Arabic and Hebrew (all provided in English
translation), we will analyze the intimate, everyday, and affective dimensions of carbonization and
warming, exploring how these forces shaped subjectivities and societies. Finally, we will consider how
different notions of heat and cooling technologies were tied to specific constructions of gender, race, and
class.

course_details.Overview of class: "Guns don't kill people, people kill people" (American proverb). "You are different with a gun in your hand; the gun is different with you holding it" (Bruno Latour, Pandora's Hope: Essays on the Reality of Science Studies, 179). These two sayings present diametrically opposed views of the relationship between weapons and society: one regards weapons as a neutral medium that merely executes violent human intentions, while the other attributes to them agency in shaping those very intentions. This course examines this tension through the history of violence and arms in Palestine/Israel, spanning the periods of the Ottoman Empire, British rule, and the establishment of the State of Israel up to the present day. Violence is a human experience unlike any other. It leaves deep emotional and physical imprints, and sometimes transforms the very way people perceive and sense the world. To examine this, we will engage with poetry, music, and film alongside archival sources, inquiring into how violence has shaped the subjectivities of perpetrators, victims, witnesses, and bystanders across various times and contexts. Can violence form a collective identity or experience? Rather than considering these questions abstractly, we will situate them in the material realities of technology. We will analyze how changing forms of surveillance, policing, and bombing have shaped ideas of humanity, delineating who belongs to it and who is excluded from it. Throughout the course, we will ask: What made different people at different points in time decide to use arms or object to their use? How and to what extent did the materiality of arms - their production, dissemination, design, or operation - influence these choices?

The course is designed with three key objectives in mind:
1) to explore how arms shaped and were shaped by the social and cultural history of Palestine/Israel
2) to examine diverse perspectives on arms production and use as experienced and enacted by various
historical actors
3) and, perhaps most crucially, to analyze how militarization has profoundly shaped the subjectivities of
those affected by it across different times and contexts.
To achieve these insights, a central aim of the seminar is to guide students in analyzing historical sources,
contextualizing them, and constructing well-founded arguments based on their analyses.

We also study scientific, legal, and pop-culture materials to elucidate what was at stake in the most heated controversies and campaigns against and in favor of the plant. We conclude analyzing the most recent debates and policies on decriminalization and

Why did South Asians migrate and settle outside South Asia? What are the historical origins of South Asian diasporic communities in Africa, South-east Asia, Europe, and North America? How did South Asia's encounter with colonialism affect the migration of South Asians elsewhere? In this thematic survey, we will learn about the history of South Asians' migration from the nineteenth century to the present, with special emphasis on the historical inter-relatedness of migration, colonialism, and decolonization. Our cast of characters will range from soldiers and exiles to laborers and merchants. We will traverse a diverse array of geographies, ranging from Singapore and Fiji to Uganda and Britain. We will discover how South Asian communities in various parts of the world were made and unmade by colonial economic imperatives, often exploitative trans-oceanic labor networks, and colonial categories of social identification. Instead of being erased by mid-twentieth century decolonization, South Asians' migration was reshaped by national imperatives of the ‘home' country on the one hand, and the new political and economic order of the post-World War II world on the other.

The course is divided into two parts. In Part I, we walk through the history of South Asian migration, paying attention to the changing historical contexts in which this phenomenon took place. In Part II, we dive deeper into socio-religious characteristics of South Asian migrants, such as caste hierarchies and gender relations, and examine why these features have persisted, and been reinvented in some instances, despite centuries of habitation outside South Asia.

course_details.Overview of class:
This course examines the recent past that most U.S. history courses never get around to discussing, the years between 1968 and 2016, when the institutions, structures, practices, and ideas that governed the United States and the world since the 1930s came undone and collapsed. The second half of a two-quarter sequence titled "The Rise and Fall of the American Century," it surveys the erosion in systems of centralized coordination and command that were created during and after World War II to explain rising inequality, mass migrations, globalization, political extremism, and the end of the Cold War, along with social isolation and atomization. Rather than seek monocausal explanations for such things, it connects political and economic changes to social and cultural shifts to explain how the past gave rise to the present. It begins with Richard Nixon's efforts to salvage U.S. power during the Vietnam War and ends with Donald Trump's attempt to make America great again only to hasten the end of the American Century.

In addition to its topical and analytical concerns, the course considers the challenges and rewards of studying the recent past. It relies on primary sources more than published history and offers students an opportunity to write a short original research paper on a subject of their choice. Prior collegiate or AP coursework in modern U.S. and/or world history will be helpful to your understanding of course materials but is not required nor necessary.

course_details.Overview of class:
History of Modern France: The French Revolution and Napoleon

The French Revolution of 1789 marks one of the major events in world history, traditionally regarded as the transition to the modern era in western historical narratives. It has also remained a subject of historical debate for more than two centuries. Why and how did an upheaval that started in Europe's largest and wealthiest country in 1789 lead to the destruction of a social system, the beheading of a king, decades of war, and the crowning of an emperor? Beginning with the reign of Louis XIV and the movement of ideas known as the Enlightenment and continuing through the Revolution and the Napoleonic Empire, this course examines the political, social, and cultural history of France during this transformative period. It also situates the Revolution in its broader Atlantic context by considering its relationship with the unprecedented 1791 slave uprising in Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, which culminated in the founding of the Republic of Haiti. Alongside larger developments, we will look at the lives of ordinary people and influential figures like Voltaire, Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette, Maximilien Robespierre, Toussaint Louverture, and Napoleon Bonaparte. Guided by Alexis de Tocqueville's enduring question-why did the French get rid of their king only to end up with an emperor?-the course investigates both the revolutionary changes and continuities of the era. Along the way, students will engage with questions about why revolutions break out, how they unfold, and why they end, examining the roles of social conflict, political institutions, ideas, contingency, and global forces in shaping one of the most consequential periods in modern history.
course_details.Learning Objectives: In this course, you will learn about France in the prerevolutionary and revolutionary period and the Napoleonic era. In addition, however, this course is designed to help students learn and think about historical change: What are different ways of thinking about a historical event, about historical causality, about the roles of different groups and individuals? How do different approaches such as social, political, gender, and global history shed different light on aspects of a historical event? How might we apply those insights to understanding the world around us?

course_details.Overview of class: This seminar introduces students to major themes in the history of Syria and other Arab-majority areas during and after WWI (1916-1920)—arguably one of the most pivotal periods in modern Middle Eastern history. Ultimately, the course is about the ways in which different historians have understood and interpreted the events that unfolded during this time period. Imagine that you and your classmates are a group of conscientious lawyers examining a case ahead of a trial. In this hypothetical scenario, one party has put forward a case based on a certain narrative of events. Out of concern for its accuracy and plausibility, your task is to determine if, or to what extent, it holds water. The case in question has been put forward by historian Elizabeth Thompson in a book dealing with Syria and the Arabs' quest for independence following WWI. We are going to familiarize ourselves with the facts of the case and the case itself. course_details.Overview of class:
Sex and Nazi Germany: two charged topics. What do they have to do with each other? More than you might think. The Nazis cared a great deal about sex. Decisions about who should have children, and who should be sterilized, sat at the center of racial policy. Brothels were set up for soldiers and for forced laborers in concentration camps. Paragraph 175 sent thousands of gay men to prison and then to the camps as well. At the same time, ordinary Germans were promised pleasure, a right extended to "Aryans" and withheld from Jews and other "undesirables." Sex had a purpose for the Third Reich: it fed the birth rate, enforced labor discipline, lifted military morale, and fueled racial war. Racism, Dagmar Herzog writes, has always also been about sex. Under National Socialism this was true in the extreme.

Studying who could have sex—or change sex—and how in the Third Reich tells us as much about racial purity, biopolitics, national identity, and state policy, as sex itself. We will cover the sexual cultures of Weimar Berlin, Nazi reproductive and racial policy, the homoerotics of fascist masculinity, Nazi theories of sexuality, the persecution of gay men, lesbians, and transvestites, sexual violence in the camps, and the place of sex in the cultural memory of Nazi Germany. Students will encounter this history through court records, medical files, memoirs, photographs, film, and scholarship.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of how the Nazi state mobilized sex, gender, and sexuality to police inclusion and exclusion within German society. The course examines specific manifestations of sexual policing and incitement through law, medicine, culture, and media. By the end of the quarter, students will be able to identify how sexuality and gender operated within Nazi society—both among marginalized populations and those prioritized by the regime—and articulate informed interpretations of their historical significance. However, the learning objectives extend beyond knowledge acquisition. I am invested in cultivating broadly applicable skills: deep and close reading, critical thinking, primary-source analysis and information extraction, and the clear, sophisticated articulation of ideas and arguments in both oral and written form. These skills will be practiced in the classroom and further honed through assessment. My hope is that students will carry these skills forward as lifelong tools for navigating the complexities of the present and the future.

course_details.Overview of class: The aim of this seminar is to introduce students to the history and historiography of race and gender during the Holocaust. As in many historical contexts, race and gender interacted dynamically and created the particular context of Nazi-occupied Europe, which was a place where Jewish men and women suffered in particular ways, German men and women participated in particular ways, and other racial groups - men and women alike - were targeted, collaborated, resisted and rescued. We will read a variety of texts that explore the influences that shaped the behavior and response of an array of people during the Holocaust. Racism sat directly in the center of the Nazi world view. Once the Nazis got into power, they sought to translate ideology into policy. Still, their racial policies evolved over time, spurred by opportunism, innovation, and war. And too, Jewish men and women responded in ways similar and divergent to the Nazi onslaught. Sexism was also seemingly an important aspect of the Nazi perspective. While they indeed embraced an anti-feminist stance, the Nazis nevertheless sought to incorporate "German" women into the national community and women participated actively in the implementation of Nazi racism.

course_details.Overview of class: Autobiography, and Jewish autobiography in particular, presents a fascinating, in most cases unparalleled opportunity to look at history and historical realities through the lens of a private individual. course_details.Overview of class: This course is an upper-level seminar that offers an upside-down examination of the Korean War highlighting the narratives of Korean people, be they North Koreans, South Koreans, adoptees, mixed race Koreans, North Korean refugees, koryo saram, chosunjok, Korean Americans, Zainichi, or POW repatriation refusers.. It begins with an examination of the physical devastation of the war and the targeted use of methods and materials such as carpet bombing and napalm and then moves to a discussion of the ideological warfare tactics honed in the war's interrogation rooms. After a brief discussion of the two nation-states that emerged from the war, the course delves into the new categories of Koreans created by the war: Amerasians, adoptees, military brides, and Zainichi returnees to North Korea. The course concludes with an examination of the Korean War in memory, both collective and individual. The course draws on oral history interviews conducted by the instructor with military brides in the United States, Zainichi Koreans in Japan, and North Korean refugees in China and will include several assignments asking students with Korean language skills to listen to and analyze interview excerpts.

course_details.Overview of class:
This class engages the "spatial turn" in the humanities and social sciences by examining influential arguments about cities as fundamental to the modernist progress or retrogression of society in the 19th, 20th, and early 21st centuries. According to many influential social science and literary manifestoes, urban development provides the quintessence of national and greater civilizational progress - or regress. We will start by considering how the theoretical literature on "urban space" can complement and transform "urban history" and examine paradigmatic Euro-American conceptions of "the modern city." We will then explore how notions of modern urbanism have had a very different effect and reception in Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

We will gain a nuanced appreciation for key theoretical approaches of "spatial-turn"-inflected scholarship on modern urbanism. We will also critically evaluate the varying ways that "urban modernity" has been appropriated and transformed in cities around the world during the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries.

course_details.Overview of class: How does our understanding of global history change when we foreground law? To what extent have international legal regimes arisen out of imperial and national dynamics? Why have slavery and settler colonialism been so important to so many constitutional and state histories? This course takes up these and other questions in order to make sense of the interplay between laws, nations, and empires around the world over the last five centuries (circa 1500 to 2000). The topics we will likely examine include: 1) the origins and effects of mixed jurisdictions (or legal pluralism) in different regions; 2) the ways empires have shaped key concepts of sovereignty, personhood, and citizenship; 3) the role of transnational corporations in bolstering imperial and national rule; 4) the history of human rights and global governance; 5) tensions between scientific and legal definitions of race and ancestry; 6) histories of Islamic law; 7) entanglements between cultural and intellectual property; 8) shifting legal definitions of indigeneity; and 9) space law and AI.
course_details.Learning Objectives: To increase your knowledge of global and transnational history; to deepen your understanding of the historical interplay among law, empire, and global governance; and to refine your expository writing skills.

Professor Lina Britto is a Colombian-American historian and journalist. She received her Ph.D. in Latin American and Caribbean History from New York University and was a postdoctoral fellow at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies, Harvard University. She is the author of Marijuana Boom: The Rise and Fall of Colombia's First Drug Paradise (University of California Press, 2020), and co-editor of Histories of Solitude and Histories of Perplexity, two volumes on Colombia, 19th to 21st centuries (Routledge, 2024). course_details.Overview of class: Modern Latin America Field Seminar introduces graduate students to some of the principal topics, debates, and literatures about the region's history since the Age of Revolutions to the neoliberal turn. It covers the most important economic, political, social, and cultural questions. It also analyzes the methodological strategies used by historians while writing about different countries. The course does not pretend to be inclusive of all historical approaches. Rather, it aims to introduce students to some of the most relevant historiographical discussions and invite them to go beyond narrow North American points of view about the neighbors to the South. The course helps students in training to become instructors to examine how Latin Americans view themselves and understand the region's histories under different lenses.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The course is thus designed to further our study and understanding of the historiography, meaning the different ways scholars have written about and conceived of Latin American history and the historical materials available. For our purposes, the substance of the books and articles selected for common reading is secondary in importance to the major themes, theoretical frameworks, source base, and methods. Students are encouraged to find their own voices and at the same time to do some justice to the works of others. Hence, the method is twofold. On the one hand, we will examine some "classic" works and influential authors in the field. On the other, we will work to find points of contact between your dissertation research and the historiography.
